finding.guards_checked: before_request load_user (views.py:10-12) does no verification; is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) is correct as a predicate but not enforcing; ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 but is used only in rename_file (views.py:26), not here.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. load_user (views.py:10-12) only copies the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header and enforces nothing. is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) is a bool predicate, and its result is discarded at views.py:18. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10), which aborts 403, is used only in rename_file (views.py:26), not in delete_file.
verdict.reason: delete_file (views.py:18) calls require_allowed, which is acl.is_allowed (acl.py:5), and discards the returned bool, so del STORE[fid] at views.py:19 runs for any caller who can send DELETE /files/<fid>.

finding.claim: Identity is taken verbatim from a client-supplied header, so any client can impersonate any user and inherit that user's grants.
finding.sink: All authorization decisions: views.py:18, views.py:26, acl.py:5, acl.py:9.

trace.note: before_request load_user registered for all routes
g.user = request.headers.get('X-Session-User-Verified') with no signature, token or session check
grants.get(user) lookup keyed on attacker-supplied name
ensure_allowed consumes the same forged identity

finding.guards_checked: None in this code. Name implies an upstream auth proxy sets the header, but the app does not confirm that. Risk drops if a trusted proxy strips and rewrites the header; deployment not confirmed.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:12 takes X-Session-User-Verified verbatim into g.user with no signature, token, or session check. acl.py:5 (is_allowed) and acl.py:9-10 (ensure_allowed) use that value as the grants key. views.py:18 and views.py:26 call them with no other check. The only possible control is an upstream proxy that strips and rewrites the header, and nothing in this repo configures or confirms one.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the code: views.py:12 copies the client-controlled header into g.user, and acl.py:5 and acl.py:9 authorize against it, so any client that can reach the app can send any user name and inherit that user's grants at views.py:18 and views.py:26. The verdict depends on deployment: if a trusted proxy strips this header before the app sees it, the finding drops, but that proxy is not in the repo and I could not confirm it.

finding.claim: rename_file stores any JSON value as the file name with no type or length validation; a missing 'name' key or non-JSON body raises unhandled errors.
finding.sink: f['name'] assignment at views.py:27 (in-memory STORE record).

trace.note: request.json['name'] assigned directly to f['name']; KeyError on missing key yields 500

finding.guards_checked: ensure_allowed correctly aborts 403 (acl.py:8-10). No type, length or schema validation on name. No sink within this code, so impact depends on consumers.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed at views.py:26 (acl.py:8-10) aborts with 403 when the user lacks the 'write' grant, so only a user with write on the file reaches line 27. No type, length, or schema validation exists on request.json["name"] at views.py:27.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate for views.py:27: any JSON value is assigned to f["name"] with no validation, and a missing key raises KeyError (500), while an attacker needs only a write grant that ensure_allowed (views.py:26, acl.py:8-10) already enforces. The candidate's "non-JSON body raises unhandled errors" half is inaccurate, since Flask returns handled 400/415 responses for that case, and the impact is limited to data-integrity and robustness with no in-code sink, so this is low severity rather than a security flaw.

finding.claim: Unknown file id raises KeyError, returning 500 instead of 404; once F1 is fixed, 403 for existing ids versus 500 for missing ids reveals whether an id exists.
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookups at views.py:17 and views.py:25.

trace.note: f = STORE[fid] raises KeyError for unknown id

finding.guards_checked: None. No existence check or 404 handling.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:17 and views.py:25 are bare `STORE[fid]` lookups with no membership check or 404 handler. Flask turns the uncaught KeyError into a 500. The ACL check runs only after the lookup, so it never gets a chance to block the missing-id case. The only guard in the path, load_user at views.py:10-12, just copies a header and does no authorization.
verdict.reason: For an existing id, rename_file reaches ensure_allowed at views.py:26, which aborts with 403 (acl.py:10) for any requester without a grant, while a missing id fails at views.py:25 with KeyError and returns 500, so an unauthenticated request already distinguishes existing from missing ids; the 500-instead-of-404 bug itself is accurate, though the claim's "once F1 is fixed" framing is unnecessary because the oracle exists now and the impact is low.
